title: Classical Athens: Democracy and Empire
summary: Mid-fifth-century Athens combined democratic participation for adult male citizens with an empire financed by tribute and sustained by naval power. The same city produced major achievements in drama, architecture, history, rhetoric, and philosophy, but women, enslaved people, resident foreigners, and allied communities stood outside or beneath its political system. Socrates' career unfolded inside this unusually argumentative civic culture, whose confidence and exclusions both shaped the controversies around him.

title: The Socratic Elenchus
summary: Socrates left no writings, so his practice must be reconstructed chiefly from Plato, Xenophon, and Aristophanes. In Plato's early dialogues he repeatedly tests claims about courage, justice, piety, and knowledge through questioning that exposes contradictions or ends in aporia. This style could be morally serious and intellectually productive, but it also embarrassed prominent Athenians and blurred, for hostile audiences, the distinction between philosophy and the sophists whom Socrates denied resembling.

title: Defeat, Oligarchy, and a Fragile Restoration
summary: The Peloponnesian War ended in 404 BC with Athens defeated, its fleet surrendered, and the Spartan-backed Thirty installed. Ancient sources attribute roughly 1,500 executions to the oligarchy before democrats restored the constitution in 403; the restoration also enacted an amnesty intended to prevent renewed civil conflict. Socrates had resisted an illegal order from the Thirty, yet his associations with Critias and Alcibiades made him politically suspect in a city still recovering from defeat and factional violence.

title: Reputation, Associations, and Old Accusations
summary: Socrates accumulated enemies through public questioning and through his association with controversial aristocrats, although describing him as their formal teacher overstates what the sources establish. Aristophanes' Clouds had already caricatured him in 423 BC as a natural philosopher and sophist, a picture Socrates later said had prejudiced jurors against him. By 399, political resentment, religious suspicion, and decades of comic and social reputation formed the background to the legal charges.

title: The Trial
summary: In 399 BC Meletus, supported by Anytus and Lycon, prosecuted Socrates for not acknowledging the city's gods, introducing new divine things, and corrupting the young. Plato's Apology presents a citizen jury—probably 501 men—finding him guilty, but the often repeated tally of 280 to 220 is a modern inference from Socrates' remarks rather than a securely recorded count. During sentencing he provocatively mentioned maintenance in the Prytaneum before eventually proposing a fine; the jury chose death, apparently by a wider margin than the conviction vote.

title: The Escape He Rejects
summary: Plato's Crito depicts Socrates' friends as ready to finance an escape and confident that practical obstacles could be overcome. Socrates refuses because he believes escaping would violate commitments he has made to Athens' laws and would damage the life of argument he has defended. The dialogue is a foundational text about political obligation, but it should not be read as a verbatim prison transcript or as proof that guards had already been bribed.

title: Death in the Phaedo
summary: Plato's Phaedo describes Socrates drinking hemlock after a final discussion about philosophy and the soul. The account ends with his request that Crito sacrifice a cock to Asclepius, a line whose meaning has generated many interpretations; the claim that Socrates simply meant life itself was an illness is influential but not certain. Plato says he was absent because he was ill, and the literary artistry of the scene cautions against treating every detail as stenographic history.

title: Plato Responds to the Execution
summary: Plato was a young member of Socrates' circle and identifies himself in the Apology among those willing to contribute to a fine. Socrates' execution plainly became a central subject of his writing and helped sharpen his distrust of political judgment, but the claim that one event alone determined everything Plato later thought goes beyond the evidence. What can be said securely is that Plato made Socrates the dominant figure in a body of dialogues that transformed a local Athenian trial into a permanent philosophical problem.

title: Plato's Dialogues
summary: About thirty-five dialogues and a collection of letters are transmitted under Plato's name, though authenticity and chronology remain disputed for some works. Early or 'Socratic' dialogues often centre on ethical questioning, while works such as Republic, Symposium, Phaedo, Timaeus, and Laws develop wider arguments in metaphysics, politics, psychology, cosmology, and education. Scholars still debate where the historical Socrates ends and Plato's own philosophy begins, which is why the dialogues preserve both a person and an unresolved interpretive problem.

title: Plato's Academy
summary: Around 387 BC Plato established a philosophical community at or near the sanctuary of Academus outside Athens. It supported sustained work in philosophy and mathematics and later counted Aristotle, Eudoxus, Speusippus, and Xenocrates among its members, but it was not a university in the modern institutional sense. The famous command excluding anyone ignorant of geometry is late and probably apocryphal, and the school suppressed under Justinian in 529 AD was a later Neoplatonic institution rather than an unbroken nine-century continuation of Plato's original Academy.

title: Aristotle at the Academy
summary: Aristotle joined Plato's Academy around 367 BC and remained in its intellectual orbit for roughly twenty years. He inherited questions and methods from Plato while developing sharply different approaches to logic, biology, physics, ethics, and metaphysics. Their disagreement cannot be reduced to Plato believing only in Forms and Aristotle believing only in particulars; Aristotle criticised separate Forms while retaining universals, causes, and explanatory structures of his own.

title: Aristotle Tutors Alexander
summary: Philip II invited Aristotle to educate the young Alexander in the 340s BC, probably at Mieza. Ancient tradition connects the curriculum with literature, ethics, politics, and medicine, but colourful details—such as a specially annotated Iliad under Alexander's pillow or specimens being dispatched to Aristotle from every campaign—come from later literary traditions and should be treated cautiously. The tutoring created a real personal and symbolic link between Greek philosophy and Macedonian power, not a simple pipeline by which Aristotle's doctrines directed Alexander's conquests.

title: The Hellenistic World
summary: Alexander's conquests and the successor kingdoms spread Greek language and institutions across Egypt and western Asia while also producing sustained encounters with Egyptian, Persian, Babylonian, Jewish, and other traditions. Koine Greek became a major language of administration, scholarship, and trade, and new centres such as Alexandria supported science, literature, and philosophy. This diffusion widened the environments in which Plato and Aristotle were copied and debated, but it was neither the first multicultural intellectual world nor a one-way export of Greek ideas.

title: Greek Philosophy in Syriac, Arabic, and Byzantium
summary: Aristotle's works survived through several overlapping traditions rather than being rescued by a single civilisation. Greek manuscripts continued to be copied in Byzantium; Syriac Christian scholars translated and taught parts of the corpus; and Abbasid-era translators rendered most of Aristotle and many commentators into Arabic. Philosophers including al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Averroes did not merely preserve these materials: they reorganised, criticised, and transformed them, while Plato's direct Arabic reception was much more limited than Aristotle's.

title: Aquinas and Latin Aristotelianism
summary: By the thirteenth century, Aristotle's works and major Arabic commentaries had entered Latin universities through translations from both Arabic and Greek. Thomas Aquinas used Aristotelian concepts in works including the Summa theologiae while revising them to fit Christian doctrines on creation, providence, soul, and God. His synthesis was enormously influential, but it was one strand within a contested medieval reception that also included Augustinian, Avicennian, Averroist, Jewish, and Byzantine traditions.

title: Whitehead's Footnotes
summary: In Process and Reality (1929), Alfred North Whitehead called the European philosophical tradition a series of footnotes to Plato. The line captures Plato's exceptional influence but is a deliberate exaggeration: European philosophy also drew deeply on pre-Socratic, Aristotelian, Stoic, Epicurean, Roman, Jewish, Christian, Islamic, and later non-European sources. Socrates' trial mattered because Plato made it a durable scene for asking how knowledge, virtue, law, and political power should relate—not because every later argument can literally be traced to one jury vote.

title: Xenophon's Socrates
summary: Xenophon's Memorabilia, Apology, Symposium, and Oeconomicus offer another literary Socrates: more practical, conventional, and advisory than the figure who develops metaphysical arguments in some Platonic dialogues. Xenophon was also defending Socrates and sometimes uses him to discuss subjects in which Xenophon himself had expertise, so he is not a neutral witness. Comparison among Xenophon, Plato, Aristophanes, and later testimony creates the enduring 'Socratic problem': no method securely recovers the historical Socrates behind the competing portraits.

title: Ficino Translates Plato
summary: Medieval Latin readers knew only a small portion of Plato directly, even while Platonism survived through Augustine, late antique authors, and other channels. Fifteenth-century humanists obtained more Greek manuscripts and translations, and Marsilio Ficino produced the first complete Latin edition of Plato's works, published in 1484 under Medici patronage. Stories that Cosimo founded a formal new Platonic Academy after hearing Plethon are more complicated than the traditional legend, but Ficino's translations decisively broadened western European access to Plato.

title: Nietzsche's Anti-Socrates
summary: In The Birth of Tragedy (1872), Friedrich Nietzsche cast Socrates as a turning point in Greek culture, arguing that confidence in rational explanation had weakened the tragic balance of Apollonian form and Dionysian force. This was a philosophical genealogy, not a neutral historical verdict on fifth-century Athens. Its importance lies in showing that Socrates' legacy remained contestable: later thinkers could treat questioning reason as liberation, domination, decadence, or all three at once.
